explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Verse 1 says those in attendance were watching Him closely. I bet nobody in that room was paying attention to the food. When a whole table has its eyes on one guest, something is about to happen.

explanations.answer: Asking Jesus to bless the meal
explanations.explanation: That's a kind guess, but the text never has anyone ask Him for that. What it says is that those in attendance were watching Him closely. Think of a coworker who stares at you the whole meeting. That kind of watching, not a blessing request.

Close, but it's the opposite. Leaving someone alone means they get to eat in peace, and verse 1 says those in attendance were watching Him closely. Nobody in that house was minding their own business, and that's me being generous. So Jesus sits down to dinner with a lot of eyes on Him.

That's it, baker. Jesus asks, “Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath or not?” (Luke 14:3). He puts the question to the experts in the law and the Pharisees, and He puts it right out loud. A man with dropsy is standing in front of everybody, so the question is not just a theory.

Good memory for a Bible question, but that one belongs to another scene. Some people asked Him about Caesar and taxes in Matthew 22:17. Here at the dinner, the question is about healing on the Sabbath. That's the one with a man with dropsy standing right there.

That question does come up with the Pharisees, but in another scene (Mark 7:5). At this dinner, Jesus is asking about healing on the Sabbath. I know, a meal and a hand question go together like dough and an oven. Still, the question at this table is about healing.

It's the other way around. Verse 4 says, “But they remained silent.” Jesus asked the experts in the law and the Pharisees a direct question, and they gave no answer at all. That silence is the whole answer the text gives.

Right, they don't answer. Verse 4 says, “But they remained silent.” Jesus asked the experts in the law and the Pharisees straight out, and nobody spoke. I think that's a silence you could hear a cookie crumb drop in.
Yes, baker. Verse 4 says Jesus took hold of the man, healed him, and sent him on his way. Nobody answered His question, and the man left healed. Jesus did it right there at the table.

Anointing is a real thing in Scripture, but it's not what the text says here. Verse 4 says Jesus took hold of the man, healed him, and sent him on his way. So the word that fits is healed. The man with dropsy walked away different than he came.

Jesus does a lot of teaching at this dinner, but the text doesn't say He teaches this man. Verse 4 says He took hold of him, healed him, and sent him on his way. I think the man got a pretty good lesson just by being healed. The word the verse uses is healed.

Yes, baker. Jesus asks, “Which of you whose son or ox falls into a pit on the Sabbath day will not immediately pull him out?” (Luke 14:5). Notice the word immediately. Nobody in His question waits for the Sabbath to end.

It actually is true. Verse 5 says, “Which of you whose son or ox falls into a pit on the Sabbath day will not immediately pull him out?” The two things falling in are a son and an ox. And the answer in His question is immediately.

That's it. Jesus says, “When you are invited to a wedding banquet, do not sit in the place of honor…” (Luke 14:8). He noticed how the guests were picking their seats and told them a parable. The best seat in the house is the one He says to leave alone.

The front door doesn't come up in the parable. Jesus says not to sit in the place of honor, in case someone more distinguished has been invited (Luke 14:8). The spot to stay away from is the best seat. Nobody's fighting over a seat near a door anyway.

The host's family never shows up in this parable. Jesus says, “…do not sit in the place of honor…” (Luke 14:8). So the seat to leave alone is the place of honor. I think the host's family could use a seat, too.

explanations.answer: Someone more distinguished may be invited
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Jesus says not to sit there “in case someone more distinguished than you has been invited” (Luke 14:8). The host could walk over and ask you to move. Picture sitting down in the best seat and seeing a fancier guest walk in.

explanations.answer: The host may run out of room
explanations.explanation: Room isn't the problem in this parable. Verse 8 says the reason is “in case someone more distinguished than you has been invited.” The trouble is a more distinguished guest showing up after you've already taken the best seat.

explanations.answer: The other guests may get jealous
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say anything about jealousy. The reason in verse 8 is “in case someone more distinguished than you has been invited.” I think it would still be an awkward walk, but that's me, not the verse.

Yes, baker. Verse 9 says the host will tell you to give your seat away, and “in humiliation, you will have to take the last place.” You started at the top and ended at the bottom. That's a long walk with everybody watching.

The middle sounds like a polite compromise, but the verse doesn't give you one. Verse 9 says, “in humiliation, you will have to take the last place.” The host's seat swap doesn't leave any room to bargain.

The front is where you started, not where you end up. The host says, “Give this man your seat,” and then verse 9 says you “will have to take the last place.” So you lose the best seat and land in the last one.

Yes, baker. Verse 10 says that when you sit in the last place, your host may come and say, “Friend, move up to a better place.” That's the opposite of the walk of shame in verse 9. This time the host does the moving, not you.

It is true, though. Verse 10 says Jesus tells them to go and sit in the last place, “so that your host will come and tell you, ‘Friend, move up to a better place.’” The host is the one who moves you up.
That's it. Verse 10 says, “Then you will be honored in front of everyone at the table with you.” The honor comes after the host moves you up. And the whole table sees it.

Scolding is what you'd expect if you grabbed the best seat, but this is the other path. Verse 10 says you “will be honored in front of everyone at the table with you.” The host invites you up and the table sees it.

Being ignored isn't what the verse says. When the host moves you up, verse 10 says you “will be honored in front of everyone at the table with you.” The whole table sees it. Nobody is looking at their plate for this one.

Not quite. Verse 11 says, “For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and the one who humbles himself will be exalted.” The one who lifts himself up gets humbled. Being exalted goes to the one who humbles himself.

Right, baker. Jesus says, “For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and the one who humbles himself will be exalted.” (Luke 14:11). Exalting yourself leads to being humbled. It's one line, and it flips the whole seating chart.

It's the opposite. Jesus tells the host, “do not invite your friends or brothers or relatives or rich neighbors” (Luke 14:12). That's the exact guest list He says to skip. I think that's one part of the dinner nobody saw coming.

Yes, baker. Jesus says, “When you host a dinner or a banquet, do not invite your friends or brothers or relatives or rich neighbors.” (Luke 14:12). That's the guest list He says to skip. I'd love to have seen the host's face.

explanations.answer: They may invite him in return
explanations.explanation: That's it. Jesus says, “Otherwise, they may invite you in return, and you will be repaid.” (Luke 14:12). If they invite you back, you've been repaid right there. It's like trading dinners and calling it even.

No-shows aren't the reason in the text. Verse 12 says, “Otherwise, they may invite you in return, and you will be repaid.” The worry is that they'll pay you back. Friends who show up and then repay you are the problem here.
Gifts aren't mentioned. The reason in verse 12 is, “Otherwise, they may invite you in return, and you will be repaid.” It's the repaying that Jesus brings up. The dinner would end up as a trade.

Yes, baker. Verse 13 says, “But when you host a banquet, invite the poor, the crippled, the lame, and the blind.” Jesus flips the guest list from the people who can repay you to the people who can't. It's the same room, with a very different table.
It is true. Verse 13 says, “But when you host a banquet, invite the poor, the crippled, the lame, and the blind.” After telling the host who to skip, Jesus tells him who to invite.

explanations.answer: At the resurrection of the righteous
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Jesus says, “Since they cannot repay you, you will be repaid at the resurrection of the righteous.” (Luke 14:14). Nobody at that table can pay the host back. So the repaying comes at the resurrection of the righteous.
A Passover feast doesn't come up here. Verse 14 says, “Since they cannot repay you, you will be repaid at the resurrection of the righteous.” That's when Jesus says the repayment comes.

explanations.answer: At the end of the harvest
explanations.explanation: Harvest time is not what Jesus names. Verse 14 says, “you will be repaid at the resurrection of the righteous.” The repayment is tied to that day, not a season.

explanations.answer: Everyone who eats at the feast in God's kingdom is blessed
explanations.explanation: That's it. One of those reclining with Jesus says, “Blessed is everyone who will eat at the feast in the kingdom of God.” (Luke 14:15). He hears Jesus talk about a banquet and the resurrection, and he answers with that. And Jesus has a story ready.

explanations.answer: Only the rich will sit at the feast in God's kingdom
explanations.explanation: The guest never says that. What he says is, “Blessed is everyone who will eat at the feast in the kingdom of God.” (Luke 14:15). Jesus had just told the host to invite the poor, so that answer pulls the other way.

explanations.answer: The poor should always be served first at every feast
explanations.explanation: That's a big rule, and the guest never says it. He says, “Blessed is everyone who will eat at the feast in the kingdom of God.” (Luke 14:15). It's a blessing, not a seating rule.

Yes, baker. The servant tells those who had been invited, “Come, for everything is now ready.” (Luke 14:17). The invitation went out first, and now it's time. Everything's done and the table is waiting.

explanations.answer: Bring a gift for the host
explanations.explanation: No gift is asked for in the message. The servant says, “Come, for everything is now ready.” (Luke 14:17). The host did the preparing. All the guests have to do is come.
They'd already been invited, so this message is the call. The servant says, “Come, for everything is now ready.” (Luke 14:17). Nobody is told to wait. It's time to come.

It goes the other way. Verse 18 says, “But one after another they all began to make excuses.” They had been invited and told everything was ready, and they started giving reasons not to come. No one came right away.
Right, baker. Verse 18 says, “But one after another they all began to make excuses.” They'd been invited, and they didn't come. One excuse after another.

explanations.answer: He is going to try them out
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. He says, “I have bought five yoke of oxen, and I am going to try them out. Please excuse me.” (Luke 14:19). He just bought them and wants to test them. Five yoke is a lot of oxen to test on banquet day.

explanations.answer: He has to go sell them
explanations.explanation: He just bought them, so selling isn't the plan. He says, “I have bought five yoke of oxen, and I am going to try them out.” (Luke 14:19). His excuse is trying them out.

explanations.answer: He must find them a barn
explanations.explanation: A barn doesn't come up. His excuse is, “I have bought five yoke of oxen, and I am going to try them out. Please excuse me.” (Luke 14:19). He's going to try them out.

Yes, baker. The third man says, “I have married a wife, so I cannot come.” (Luke 14:20). Notice he says cannot, not please excuse me like the other two. Three men, three reasons, and none of them show up.
It is true. Verse 20 says, “Still another said, ‘I have married a wife, so I cannot come.’” That's the third excuse. And his version says he cannot come.
Yes, baker. Verse 21 says, “Then the owner of the house became angry.” The servant reported all of it, and that's how the owner reacts. Then he sends the servant out again.
Worry isn't what the text says. Verse 21 says, “Then the owner of the house became angry.” And then he gives the servant a new job right away.
He has plenty to say. Verse 21 says the owner “became angry” and tells his servant to go out quickly into the streets and alleys of the city. Quiet is not how this master handles it.

explanations.answer: The same people Jesus told the host to invite
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The owner says to bring in “the poor, the crippled, the blind, and the lame.” (Luke 14:21). Earlier Jesus told the host to invite “the poor, the crippled, the lame, and the blind” (Luke 14:13). That's the same group, in the story as well as at the real dinner table.

explanations.answer: The leaders and teachers of the city
explanations.explanation: The leaders and teachers aren't on the list. The owner says, “Go out quickly into the streets and alleys of the city, and bring in the poor, the crippled, the blind, and the lame.” (Luke 14:21). It's the same group Jesus named to the host in verse 13.

explanations.answer: The friends of the guests who said no
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't name them. The owner sends his servant for “the poor, the crippled, the blind, and the lame.” (Luke 14:21). That echoes the guest list Jesus gave the host in Luke 14:13.

Yes, baker. The master says, “Go out to the highways and hedges and compel them to come in…” (Luke 14:23). The servant already did the streets and alleys, and there's still room. So the search goes further out.
The temple courts don't come up in the story. The master says, “Go out to the highways and hedges…” (Luke 14:23). That's farther out than the streets and alleys.
The city gates aren't named. The servant is told, “Go out to the highways and hedges…” (Luke 14:23). The search has moved out past the city streets.

That's it. The master says, “…so that my house will be full.” (Luke 14:23). The servant said there was still room, and the master wants none left. Think of a cookie jar he plans to see packed to the brim.
Cleanliness isn't what the master cares about here. He says, “…so that my house will be full.” (Luke 14:23). He wants every seat taken.
Quiet is the opposite of what a full house sounds like. The master says, “…so that my house will be full.” (Luke 14:23). I think a full house would be a loud, happy one.

It goes the other way. The master says, “For I tell you, not one of those men who were invited will taste my banquet.” (Luke 14:24). The men invited first are the ones who made excuses. Their seats get filled by others.

Right, baker. The master says, “For I tell you, not one of those men who were invited will taste my banquet.” (Luke 14:24). They were invited first and gave their excuses. That's where Jesus ends the story.
